text:
jamie: us-west2 reporting ~35% GPU capacity drop after provider maintenance, autoscaler brought nodes but latency spiked. Noticed weird client distribution — some clients still resolving to the old us-west2 IPs despite failover. Suspect DNS cache stickiness at ISP level. Need a plan: TTL tuning? CDN steering? :eyes:
ashley: seeing bursts of 5xx and GPU OOMs on us-west2 pods. Started redirect to standby pool (us-east1) but traffic is split — ~60/40 in favor of old ips. Opened runbook incident.
lee: ran quick checks — dig from multiple resolvers returns mixed answers. Example: `dig +short @8.8.8.8 inference.redwood.ai A` -> returns old IP for me. Some public resolvers still honoring previous RR weight.
maria: @lee can you paste output of `dig +trace`? also confirm if DNS provider applied new health checks/failover weights or if it was a cname swap that may be cached.
lee: paste: ```; ;; QUESTION SECTION: inference.redwood.ai. IN A; ;; ANSWER SECTION: inference.redwood.ai. 300 IN A 35.198.21.7 ; ;; AUTHORITY SECTION: ...``` — but some resolvers show 3600 TTL. Looks like upstream partly ignored our TTL change.
tariq: FYI — provider maintenance may have changed authoritative NS behavior briefly. I've started a support ticket with provider NOC (INC-4321) asking for cache flush on their anycast front. They acknowledged and are investigating.
nashley: short-term mitigation ideas: (1) try emergency TTL downshift to 60s, (2) push CDN edge steering to prefer us-east1 for rw endpoints, (3) mark affected us-west2 nodes draining and cordon to reduce client affinity, (4) notify customers on status page. Thoughts? :+1:
jamie: agree with steps but note: lowering TTL mid-incident often doesn't help full-mesh — downstream ISP resolvers can ignore it until refresh. We should rely on CDN/edge steering + backend draining as primary. Keep DNS change as secondary.
deploy-bot: failover-route applied -> route: inference.redwood.ai weight(us-east1)=80 weight(us-west2)=20 by automation at 1979012362
maria: started CDN steering rule: if geo=NA then prefer us-east1 origin, and added header `x-redwood-failover: us-east1`. Purged CDN for `/*` to accelerate.
lee: ran `curl -I https://inference.redwood.ai/health -H "Host: inference.redwood.ai"` from 3 vantage points — us-east1 now responds faster, us-west2 still serving some traffic. Logged to #metrics: 95th latency for us-west2 increased from 110ms -> 420ms.
tariq: cost note — moving large traffic to us-east1 increases egress & spot GPU costs. We'll track burn and consider rebalancing via weighted routing to avoid doubling spend. Create cost alert for >20% delta.
ashley: action item list for post-incident: 1) update DNS failover section of runbook (add clear guidance: do not rely on TTL only; prefer CDN steering + LB weight changes), 2) add checklist for contacting provider NOC and escalate contacts, 3) pre-authorize emergency TTL change to 30s (with approval path), 4) pre-warm standby pools in other regions during announced maint windows.
jamie: quick commands we ran / recommended (copy into runbook):
```
# check public resolutions
dig +short @8.8.8.8 inference.redwood.ai A
# full trace to see authoritative chain
dig +trace inference.redwood.ai
# check CDN edge resolution
curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null https://inference.redwood.ai/health -H "Host: inference.redwood.ai"
# temporarily adjust DNS weight
dnsctl set-weight inference.redwood.ai us-east1 80
# CDN purge
cdnctl purge --pattern "inference.redwood.ai/*"
```
lee: misc note — add a paragraph explaining why aggressive TTL downshift during incidents can backfire: many ISPs respect previously cached RRs until TTL expiry or have min-TTL clamps. Also some resolvers will respect SOA/negative caching.
maria: I'll draft the runbook changes and PR to /docs/runbooks/dns-failover.md, include sample commands and emergency contacts.
ashley: good job team. keeping this thread open until provider confirms caches cleared. I'll update status page and send a short customer note if we see >15% error rate sustained. :loudspeaker:
jamie: closing notes: post-incident retrospective to include network diagrams showing where DNS is cached (provider edge, ISP resolvers, client local caches) and example timelines for expected propagation. Also recommend a quarterly test of failover paths with controlled canary traffic. :memo:
